Safety and supervision

For young shooters the safety rules are the same as for adults, but supervision is closer. In lessons and training a coach or instructor stands right next to the child on the stand, close enough to take hold of the gun at any moment. A child is never left alone with a gun, at the shooting ground or at home.

A competition works differently: the referee runs the stand, and nobody may coach the shooter. Age limits and supervision rules for minors depend on your country’s law and on the ground’s own rules: see Documents and licences.

Before the first shot, the child should know the core rules from The core safety rules. The muzzle points in a safe direction. The gun stays open when not shooting. Cartridges go in only on the stand, when the coach says so. On “Stop!” (cease fire) the gun is opened and everyone waits.

Tip: A useful check: ask the child to explain these rules in their own words before each of the first sessions.

A child who shoots always wears hearing protection and safety glasses, like any shooter. For children who come to watch near a layout (the shooting area with its stands and traps), the rules differ a little between the disciplines.

Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™

Children at the shooting ground, outside the clubhouse, wear hearing protection at all times. Glasses are compulsory for anyone close to a stand.

Compak® Sporting

Hearing protection is compulsory for all spectators near the layout, children included. Glasses are compulsory for competitors, referees and staff.

Tip: Buy protection in children’s sizes: muffs that are too big slip and protect poorly. Many coaches also ask children to wear glasses whenever they stand near a stand, whatever the discipline.

Tiredness is the enemy of safety. When a child is tired, cold or too hot, attention drops, and then it is better to stop. Plan short sessions with breaks, and bring water, a hat and a snack.

At home, store the gun and cartridges as the law of your country requires. Usually that means a locked safe, cartridges kept separately and keys held only by adults. A child has no access to guns without an adult.

Parents at the ground set an example too. Stand behind the stand, keep quiet during a shot, do not touch other people’s guns and wear ear and eye protection yourself. Children often copy what they see adults do.

Key points

  • In lessons and training, a coach stands right next to the child on the stand
  • The same safety rules as for adults, explained before the first shot
  • Ear and eye protection in a child’s size
  • A tired child means the session is over
  • At home, guns and cartridges are locked away as the law requires

Did you know?

A shotgun shot reaches about 160–170 dB at the shooter's ear at its loudest instant (decibels, dB, measure loudness). For one short, sharp bang like this the upper limits are 140 dB for adults and 120 dB for children. The adult limit comes from workplace safety rules, and the WHO recommends the one for children. That is why children who only watch need ear protection too.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Where should the coach be while a child is shooting in a training session?

    1. Behind the squad, where he can watch the whole stand
    2. Right beside the child, able to take the gun at once
    3. At the trap, ready to stop the targets
    Answer

    Right beside the child, able to take the gun at once

    In training, direct supervision means the coach stands next to the child and can step in at once. In a competition the referee runs the stand.

  2. Your daughter only comes to watch a competition. Does she need hearing protection?

    1. Yes, the rules require it near the layout
    2. No, only the people who are shooting need it
    3. Only if she stands right next to the stand
    Answer

    Yes, the rules require it near the layout

    Both rulebooks require hearing protection for spectators near the layout; in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ children outside the clubhouse wear it at all times.

  3. What should you do when a child gets tired during a session?

    1. Add one more round to build character
    2. Switch to a harder target to keep interest
    3. Stop the session: tiredness lowers attention
    Answer

    Stop the session: tiredness lowers attention

    When attention drops the risk of a gun-handling mistake rises, so it is better to stop.
